title: Mossy and Drift's Starry Sled Ride
markdown:
Some evenings wear a hush that feels like a gift. This was one of those evenings in the Whispering Woods. Stars lay scattered like chips of ice on dark velvet, and the frost had that clean sting that makes a nose tingle. Mossy the moose calf stood in the snow with steam rising from his muzzle. His antlers were still only nubs, pale and new. Beside him Drift the snowshoe hare twitched long soft ears. His feet were so broad and white they looked like two small cloud-boots.

“Grandma Fir’s cabin is always so cozy,” Drift whispered, voice like dry leaves. “Especially when she bakes those blueberry scones. Warm little pillows.”

Mossy nodded. His eyes shone like polished acorns. “And her hot chocolate. It is like drinking a hug. It chases the shivers right out.”

A wooden sled waited between them, piled with a wool blanket, a sticky jar of honey, a bag of crunchy salty nuts, and—most precious of all—Grandma Fir’s favourite berry jam. The cabin lay deep in the woods, a place where the fire always seemed to be burning.

Then the sky began to shimmer. Soft green first, then a swirl of violet, then a ribbon of rose. The aurora unrolled above the dark trees as if someone had taken a brush to the night. Beautiful, yes. And late. Time was slipping.

“The aurora,” Drift squeaked, whiskers quivering. “Grandma Fir will be waiting.”

Mossy looked at the loaded sled. He imagined the weight of it and felt his own legs go wobbly, like uncooked spaghetti. “I do not know, Drift. That sled looks awfully heavy.”

Drift, usually a bounce of hops, edged closer. “And the path looks slippy. My feet are perfect for leaping. Pulling is a different sort of hop. Like dancing in moonbeams.”

It is easy to feel small when a big job stands in front of you. That is when friendship behaves like a lantern. Mossy looked at Drift’s drooping ears and felt a warmth start in his chest. Drift looked up at Mossy’s kind worried face and knew they had to try.

“We’ll do it together,” Mossy said, finding a sliver of courage that felt as solid as oak. “I’ll pull. You guide. Push with those speedy feet when it gets tricky.”

Drift’s ears sprang up like flags. “Yes. I’ll hop ahead and scout for ice.”

They hitched the rope to Mossy’s collar. With a heave the sled creaked, groaned, and moved. Drift loped alongside, fluffy feet almost silent, calling in a high clear voice. “A little left, Mossy. Root under the snow there.”

It was not easy. The path bucked. The sled tilted and threatened to spill its cargo. Once Drift hopped too hard from behind and landed in a heap of prickly pinecones. He wriggled and giggled as they stuck to his nose and ears. Mossy let out a rumbling chuckle that shook his whole body. “You look like a walking pine tree.”

Then came a small icy hill. Mossy dug his hooves in. His muscles strained. The air tasted sharp as frost. Drift scrambled to the back, braced his hind legs, and pushed. Scrape. Scrape. Push. Inch by inch they climbed. “We’re doing it,” Drift panted, breath puffing in white clouds.

They reached a wide meadow. The snow here was deep and soft, a giant carpet that swallowed sound. For a moment they paused, just to look. The aurora spread in its full glory—emerald, violet, a hint of rose—dancing as if the sky itself had learned a reel. Mossy tasted frost on his tongue. Drift’s ears stood so still the lights seemed to pour into them. Then a gust swept through, cold and sharp as an icy finger. It tugged the blanket and made the lights flicker, as if they were growing tired.

“The wind,” Mossy grunted, leaning into the pull. “It’s pushing us back.”

The lights dimmed. A shiver that was not only cold ran down his spine. Then, as he tried to turn from a sideways buffet, the sled tipped. With a sickening thump the jam jar tumbled off, rolled, and vanished into the shadows at the wood’s edge.

Mossy stopped. His breath caught. “Oh no.” His ears drooped. He had not been strong enough. He had failed.

Drift’s hops turned trudgy. He looked at the empty place on the sled, then at his friend’s hanging head. He knew what that jam meant. “It’s all gone,” he mumbled, and a tear made a tiny damp spot on his cheek.

They stood while the wind whistled a lonely tune and the last glow of the aurora thinned to a pale whisper. The warmth from earlier seemed to have gone out.

Then Drift’s keen eyes caught a faint wavering shimmer at the meadow’s edge, by a patch of moss. Glow-worms. And nestled beside their soft green lamps, glinting, was the jam jar.

“Mossy! Look. The jam. The glow-worms are lighting it.”

Mossy lifted his head. His ears swivelled. He trotted over, hooves crunching, and nudged the jar with his nose, rolling it gently so it would not crack. Drift scooped it up with quick paws and set it in the very centre of the sled, patting it down.

“We can still do it,” Mossy said. The wobble had left his voice. Warmth came back—not only from the thought of Grandma Fir’s fire, but from Drift, who had not given up. “Together.”

“Together,” Drift said, ears tall.

They hitched the sled again. This time Mossy plodded with a steady gait, hooves finding better purchase. Drift ran beside him, pushing and steering, finding the safest line through the soft snow. The wind still blew, but it seemed less mean. The aurora painted one last fleeting smile across the sky.

Through the dark trees they saw a warm glow. Grandma Fir’s cabin. With one last push from Drift and a powerful pull from Mossy, the sled slid to a halt by her door.

Grandma Fir opened it, face alight, eyes twinkling like the stars. “Oh, my dears. You made it. Just as the last of the fairy lights danced away.” She hugged Mossy so tight his antlers tickled her nose, then scooped Drift into a fuzzy embrace.

Inside, the fire crackled. Shadows danced on the walls. The smell of fresh scones filled the room, blueberries and butter and a hint of woodsmoke. Grandma Fir set out three cups and the rescued jam. They sat on a soft rug with rich hot chocolate and the jam spread thick on warm scones. Mossy’s wobbly legs felt steady at last. Drift’s pinecone stickiness had been combed out, though one tiny scale still clung behind an ear, and Grandma Fir pretended not to notice. Mossy looked at Drift, and Drift looked at Mossy. They had not only hauled a sled. They had hauled their courage and their friendship all the way to that door. The hardest journeys, they decided, often bring the sweetest rewards. They both smiled—a true friendship smile.
